html:
In 138 BCE the Chinese envoy Zhang Qian left the capital of the Han dynasty to find allies in the far west. His journey, and his reports on what he found, opened Chinese contact with Central Asia.

Emperor Wu wanted to fight the Xiongnu nomads. He sent Zhang Qian to find the Yuezhi, whom the Xiongnu had driven west, and win them as allies. On the way the Xiongnu captured him and held him for about ten years; he married there and had a son.

He escaped and travelled on to Dayuan in the Fergana Valley, famous for its horses, and to the Yuezhi, who by then lived in Bactria. They were settled and comfortable and had no wish for revenge. Caught again on the way home, he got back to China in 126 BCE with only one of his hundred companions.

His reports told the court of rich cities, fine horses, Parthia and India. The emperor sent more envoys and armies west, including the War of the Heavenly Horses. This is why Zhang Qian is often called the man who opened the Silk Road.
